title: Beauty and ugliness together
hook: when all know beauty as beauty, ugliness appears; the sage teaches without words (Tao Te Ching 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Tao that can be told: chapter one's warning that any way you can tell isn't the whole of it. Your line was not the one that can be told.
screen: `NOT THE ONE THAT CAN BE TOLD.`

segments.voice: A grandmother at a stove. She has never once given a cooking lesson. No recipe card, no lecture on salt. But a child stands at her elbow most evenings, watching her hands: the pinch, the stir, the way she tastes and waits and tastes again. Years later that child cooks the same dish, the hands move the same way, and nobody remembers being taught. Chapter two of the Tao Te Ching ends on that kind of teaching. It gets there by way of beauty, and its shadow.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER AT A STOVE.` → `NO RECIPE, NO LECTURE.` → `THE HANDS REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: First, beauty makes ugliness. Legge's translation opens: "All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful," and in knowing it, they also get the idea of ugliness. Crown one thing beautiful and you've drawn a line; everything on the other side becomes the ugly. Name the skillful, and the clumsy appear. Second, pairs that need each other. The chapter lists them: what is and what isn't, hard and easy, long and short, high and low, notes and tones that make harmony together, front and back. Each half is only known by the other. That's not a complaint about the world. It's how naming works: every word comes with its opposite attached. Third, without the use of speech. So what does the wise person do? In Legge's words, the sage "manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech." Not lazy: without forcing, without the extra layer of pointing, labeling and grading. The teaching is in how the work is done. Fourth, the work stays. The sage does the work and doesn't claim it, the chapter says, and because nothing is claimed, nothing is taken away. A grandmother doesn't sign the dish. It goes on being made anyway.
screen: `BEAUTY MAKES UGLINESS.` · `PAIRS THAT NEED EACH OTHER.` · `WITHOUT THE USE OF SPEECH.` · `THE WORK STAYS.` · then, large: `WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you'd like the people around you to learn: patience in traffic, the phone down at dinner, a thank-you at the counter. Instead of planning what to say about it, picture yourself simply doing it, quietly, with nobody told, and hold that picture while you breathe. If you pray, you can ask for help with it; if not, rehearse it in your body.
Beauty and ugliness together. Chapter two's warning that every name brings its opposite with it, and its picture of a teacher who teaches without words. Today's word.
Your line: without words. The dish gets passed on, and nobody signs it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Taoist teaching, the sage's 'teaching without words' is often read as teaching by example: a teacher who lives the Way so that students learn from watching rather than from instruction.

chat.says: What does it mean to teach without words?
options: Teaching by how you do the work, without forcing or labeling, and without claiming it.
Staying silent, so people have to work everything out on their own.
Doing nothing at all, and trusting that things will sort themselves out.
chat.meaning: Chapter two's sage conveys instructions without the use of speech: not lazy, but without forcing. The teaching is in how the work is done.
